title: Raga Basant
hook: the raga of spring, and a line about a month when it is always spring

segments.voice: Yesterday, Namdev's cup of milk in Bhairao, and your line was the milk offering. What did you hand to someone as if it would really be received? A new week starts now. Day one thousand one hundred fourteen.

Somewhere in the Guru Granth Sahib there's a line that does something strange to the calendar. It praises a month, then says that in this month spring is always present. Always. Not for a few weeks between the cold and the heat. Not until the blossoms drop. A spring that doesn't end. It's the opening of today's raga, Basant, the raga of spring, which tradition sings when the actual spring comes round. So there are two springs in this section. One arrives with the season. The other, the Granth suggests, is something else entirely. Today: Raga Basant.
screen: `A MONTH WHEN SPRING IS ALWAYS PRESENT.` → `TWO SPRINGS.` → `RAGA BASANT.`

segments.voice: Where we are: Basant comes right after Bhairao in the Granth's order. Basant is also an ordinary word for spring, and the raga carries the season in its name. Tradition sings it in springtime, so a raga here is not only a mood but a calendar: you'd hear these hymns as the fields turn green. Now the opening hymn, by Guru Nanak, in paraphrase. Of all the months, blessed is the month in which spring is always present. Blossom, my mind, by remembering the One. That's the first move: the Guru takes the season everyone is waiting for and makes it permanent, then hands it to the mind. The second move comes in a hymn by Guru Amar Das further into the section. In paraphrase: spring has come, and all the green growth has flowered. And these living beings flower too, when they fix their attention on God. Notice the two levels sitting side by side. Outside, a real spring, with real blossoms; the hymns don't pretend it isn't lovely. Inside, a flowering that doesn't need a date on the calendar, because it comes from where the mind rests. A field blooms once a year. The Granth's spring is always present, because the One it remembers is always present. So when the season does come round, and the gurdwara sings Basant, the outer spring becomes a reminder of the inner one. Today's line is simple: spring.
screen: `BASANT: THE SEASON IN THE NAME.` · `A MONTH WHEN SPRING IS ALWAYS PRESENT.` · `BLOSSOM, MY MIND.` · `THE FIELD BLOOMS; SO DO THE BEINGS.` · then, large: `SPRING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Basant, and look for one green thing. If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Basant. If not, sit in the quiet. Bring to mind, or look at, one living thing near you: a plant on the sill, a tree outside, even a weed in a crack of the pavement. Notice that it is growing right now, too slowly to see. Breathe slowly with it. Then turn the same attention inward, gently, without forcing anything to bloom. If you pray, you can remember the One the way Guru Nanak's line asks: blossom, my mind. If you don't, simply rest with the green thing. The bell holds the time.
Raga Basant. The raga of spring, which follows Bhairao, sung by tradition in the spring season, and opening with Guru Nanak's month in which spring is always present. Today's word.
Your line: spring. Whatever the season outside your window, find one thing today that's quietly growing, and give it a second look. Day one thousand one hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: In kirtan, shabads from the Basant section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Basant, and tradition gives the raga a special place in the spring season.
